Respiratory Virus Outbreak Disrupts Electrical Equipment Industry in Jordan

A respiratory virus outbreak has struck the Electrical Equipment industry in Jordan, causing significant operational disruptions and raising concerns about worker safety and production continuity, industry sources said this week.

The outbreak, first identified last week at the Amman production complex of Jordan ElectroTech Solutions, has since spread to at least three other major manufacturing sites in the Zarqa and Irbid regions, according to the Jordan Electrical Equipment Manufacturers Association (JEEMA). As of Tuesday, over 120 workers across the sector have tested positive for the virus, with several dozen more in isolation awaiting test results, union representatives report.

“Production lines have slowed dramatically at several key facilities as precautionary measures are implemented and staff shortages mount,” said Ahmad Salameh, spokesperson for JEEMA. “Some companies have temporarily reduced shifts or suspended certain processes altogether until the situation stabilizes.”

Industry insiders note that assembly lines for circuit breakers, switchgear, and power distribution panels have been particularly affected, with absenteeism rates rising sharply since the start of the outbreak. At National Electrotech Manufacturing’s Zarqa site, management confirmed that output has dropped by nearly 30 percent compared to the previous month due to the high number of workers in quarantine and increased cleaning protocols.

The Jordanian Ministry of Labour has dispatched inspection teams to several facilities to ensure compliance with health guidelines and has urged companies to enhance on-site screening, enforce mask mandates, and improve ventilation in production halls. “We are coordinating closely with industry leaders to safeguard workers’ health while minimizing disruptions to essential operations,” said a ministry official, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Workers’ representatives have voiced concern about the pace of response measures. “Our members are worried about their safety, especially as cases continue to rise,” said Samira Al-Qudah, a union leader at the Amman Electrical Equipment Workers Union. “We are calling for all affected sites to provide paid sick leave and immediate access to medical care.”

Despite the challenges, several firms have initiated rapid testing at entry points and staggered work shifts to limit contact among employees. However, industry analysts warn that if the outbreak persists or intensifies, further reductions in output and potential site closures cannot be ruled out.

“Given the concentration of key production facilities in Jordan, any prolonged disruption could have a lasting impact,” said Khaled Mansour, an independent industry analyst based in Amman. “The next two weeks will be critical as companies and authorities assess the effectiveness of containment efforts and adapt their operations accordingly.”
